en: Netti:
The Section on Detailed Exposition (Paṭiniddesavāra), Analysis 4.
The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Footings (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra-vibhaṅga).
Therein, what is the mode of conveying footings?
“The Victor teaches the Dhamma”—this is the mode of conveying footings.
What does it teach?
Ignorance (avijjā) has the characteristic of not fully penetrating the true nature of all phenomena; its proximate cause is the perversions (vipallāsa).
Craving (taṇhā) has the characteristic of clinging; its proximate cause is the agreeable and pleasant.
Greed has the characteristic of longing; its proximate cause is taking what is not given.
Perception of beauty has the characteristic of grasping at color, shape, and secondary sexual characteristics; its proximate cause is restraint of the sense faculties.
Perception of pleasure has the characteristic of approaching contact accompanied by taints; its proximate cause is gratification.
The perception of impermanence has the characteristic of not regarding conditioned phenomena; consciousness is its proximate cause.
The perception of self has the characteristic of not regarding the perception of suffering and the perception of impermanence; the mental body is its proximate cause.
True knowledge has the characteristic of penetrating all phenomena; everything that is to be known is its proximate cause.
Tranquility has the characteristic of withdrawing the mind from distraction; its proximate cause is foulness (asubha).
Non-greed has the characteristic of withdrawing the mind from the sphere of desire; its proximate cause is abstaining from taking what is not given.
Non-hatred has the characteristic of non-malice; its proximate cause is abstaining from the destruction of life.
Non-delusion has the characteristic of non-deviation regarding the basis; its proximate cause is right practice.
The perception of foulness has the characteristic of apprehending the livid, the festering, and so forth; its proximate cause is disenchantment.
The perception of suffering has the characteristic of full understanding of contact accompanied by taints; its proximate cause is feeling.
The perception of impermanence has the characteristic of contemplating conditioned phenomena; its proximate cause is their arising and passing away.
The perception of non-self has the characteristic of non-adherence to all phenomena; its proximate cause is the perception of phenomena.
The five strands of sensual pleasure are the proximate cause for sensual lust; the five physical faculties are the proximate cause for lust for form.
The sixth sense-base is the proximate cause for craving for existence; the contemplation of the produced existence is the proximate cause for the five aggregates of clinging;
and the knowledge and vision of recollecting past lives is the proximate cause [for the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings].
Faith has the characteristic of conviction and is manifested as resolve; serenity has the characteristic of clarity and is manifested as composure.
Faith has the characteristic of being yearned for; its proximate cause is unwavering confidence (*aveccappasāda*).
Serenity has the characteristic of being untroubled; its proximate cause is faith.
Energy has the characteristic of exertion; its proximate cause is the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*).
Mindfulness has the characteristic of not wobbling; its proximate cause is the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
Concentration has the characteristic of one-pointedness; its proximate cause is the jhānas.
Wisdom has the characteristic of discerning; its proximate cause is the truths.
Another method: unwise attention has the characteristic of attending to gratification; its proximate cause is ignorance.
Ignorance has the characteristic of deluding regarding the truths; it is the proximate cause for volitional formations.
Volitional formations have the characteristic of producing renewed existence; they are the proximate cause for consciousness.
Consciousness has the characteristic of spontaneous rebirth; it is the proximate cause for name-and-form.
Name-and-form has the characteristic of the integration of the mental body and the physical body; it is the proximate cause for the six sense bases.
The six sense bases have the characteristic of the demarcation of the faculties; they are the proximate cause for contact.
Contact has the characteristic of the coincidence of eye, visible form, and visual consciousness; it is the proximate cause for feeling.
Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing the desirable and the undesirable; it is the proximate cause for craving.
Craving has the characteristic of clinging; it is the proximate cause for clinging.
Clinging that leads to rebirth is the proximate cause for becoming.
Becoming, characterized by the manifestation of the mental body and the physical body, is the proximate cause for birth.
Birth, characterized by the appearance of the aggregates, is the proximate cause for aging.
Aging has the characteristic of the maturation of the physical basis (*upadhi*); it is the proximate cause for death.
Death has the characteristic of the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*); it is the proximate cause for sorrow (*soka*).
Sorrow is that which causes agitation; it is the proximate cause for lamentation (*parideva*).
Lamentation consisting of repeated wailing is the proximate cause of suffering.
Physical oppression is suffering; it is the proximate cause of mental grief.
Mental oppression is grief; it is the proximate cause of despair.
The fever of longing is the producer of burning; it is the proximate cause for existence (*bhava*).
When these factors of existence (*bhavaṅga*) arise together, that is existence; it is the proximate cause for the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
The Path, characterized by leading out, is the proximate cause for cessation (*nirodha*).
Knowledge of the ford is the proximate cause for knowledge of what has been drunk; knowledge of what has been drunk is the proximate cause for knowledge of the bowl;
knowledge of the bowl is the proximate cause for knowledge of oneself; knowledge of oneself is the proximate cause for having performed merit in the past;
having performed merit in the past is the proximate cause for dwelling in a suitable locality; dwelling in a suitable locality is the proximate cause for relying on true persons.
Dependence upon true persons is the proximate cause for right self-application; right self-application is the proximate cause for virtuous conduct;
virtuous conduct is the proximate cause for freedom from remorse; freedom from remorse is the proximate cause for gladness;
gladness is the proximate cause for rapture; rapture is the proximate cause for tranquility; tranquility is the proximate cause for happiness.

Happiness is the proximate cause for concentration; concentration is the proximate cause for knowledge and vision of things as they truly are; knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is the proximate cause for disenchantment;
disenchantment is the proximate cause for dispassion; dispassion is the proximate cause for liberation;
and liberation is the proximate cause for the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thus, whatever is a decisive support (upanissaya) and whatever is a condition (paccaya), all that is the proximate basis (padaṭṭhāna).
Therefore the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "The Victor teaches the Dhamma.
The Mode of Conveying the Proximate Basis is concluded.
